prompt.text:
Your task is to generate a complete research paper using the materials below.
You must produce:
1. A BibTeX bibliography file (references.bib)
2. The full LaTeX paper (template.tex)

Instructions
• Use the research idea and experimental logs to construct a coherent, rigorous ML paper.
• For related work and baselines:
  – Search for and include influential papers published up until 2024-11.
  – Incorporate relevant literature and add the corresponding BibTeX entries to references.bib.
  – Do NOT hallucinate papers or reference keys; all citation entries must be real.
• In the LaTeX paper, cite papers using \cite{} with keys that match exactly with your entries in references.bib.
• Do not fabricate experimental results or make claims unsupported by the logs.

Materials
Here are all the raw research materials to assist with the writing process:

[RESEARCH IDEA]
## Problem Statement
We aim to address the severe data burden associated with training high-quality diffusion models. Currently, producing state-of-the-art generative models requires massive datasets, which introduces exorbitant storage expenses, complex data acquisition pipelines, and strict privacy constraints. Existing knowledge distillation methods for diffusion models typically still require access to the original source data. Furthermore, they often constrain the student model to strictly inherit the architectural design of the teacher model. An alternative naive approach—using a teacher model to fully synthesize a massive replacement dataset prior to training—is computationally paralyzing due to the inherently slow, multi-step generation process of diffusion models. We need a strategy to train structurally flexible diffusion models from scratch without ever accessing or storing a dataset.

## Core Hypothesis
We hypothesize that we can use existing, pretrained diffusion models directly as continuous "data sources" to train new models of entirely different architectures in a strictly data-free manner. We propose that the most efficient medium for transferring knowledge is not fully synthesized, realistic samples, but rather the intermediate, time-domain noisy states. By forcing a student model to learn step-by-step from the active denoising trajectory of a teacher model, we can completely eliminate the reliance on real-world data while drastically reducing the time bottleneck of full sample generation.

## Proposed Methodology (High-Level Technical Approach)
We will construct a framework for data-free distillation divided into two primary logical components: an objective formulation module and a dynamic knowledge-gathering pipeline. 

**1. Data-Free Distillation Objective**
Standard diffusion training relies on ground-truth data to define the forward noise-adding process. We will reformulate the traditional optimization objective to entirely sever this dependency. Instead of pulling real samples to calculate target noise, we will use the pretrained teacher model's outputs as the definitive reference. The objective will be designed to minimize the discrepancy between the student’s predicted denoising behavior and the teacher's predicted denoising behavior. By mapping the student's learning directly to the teacher's reverse process, the student will gradually internalize the teacher’s learned data distribution without ever observing a real image. 

**2. Dynamic Iterative Distillation Pipeline**
Because extracting even partial trajectories from a teacher model can become computationally heavy, we will design an iterative extraction loop that provides an endless, efficient stream of intermediate training data.
*   *Continuous Step-by-Step Learning:* Instead of having the teacher execute long, multi-step denoising chains to build a training batch, we will initialize a batch with pure noise. In each iteration, the teacher will perform only a single denoising step. The student will immediately calculate its loss against this single step.
*   *Noise-Level Shuffling:* To ensure the student does not overfit to uniform noise states, we will introduce a randomization mechanism. This will apply varied, random denoising steps to our initial noise batch, forcing the pool to contain a highly diverse mixture of noise levels before the iterative learning begins.
*   *Dynamic Pool Management:* To maintain data diversity and mimic the random sampling of standard dataset training, we will maintain an artificially enlarged pool of these intermediate noisy samples. During each training step, a random subset will be drawn for the student to learn from. Once the teacher denoises these samples by one step, they will be cycled back into the pool. Once a sample reaches zero noise (a fully generated state), it is discarded and replaced with fresh noise, perpetuating the cycle.

## Expected Contribution
We intend to establish the first fully data-free paradigm for training diffusion models of arbitrary architectures. This approach is expected to eliminate the massive storage and acquisition costs of generative training, seamlessly bypass dataset privacy and licensing constraints, and grant researchers total architectural flexibility when designing new models, relying solely on open-source pretrained networks as synthetic environments.

[EXPERIMENTAL LOGS]
## 1. Experimental Setup

*   **Datasets:** 
    *   *Pixel Space:* CIFAR10 (32x32 resolution, 50,000 images), CelebA (64x64 resolution, 202,599 images), and ImageNet (32x32 resolution, 1,281,167 images).
    *   *Latent Space:* CelebA-HQ (256x256 resolution, 25,000 images) and FFHQ (256x256 resolution, 60,000 images).
*   **Evaluation Metrics:** 
    *   Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) served as the primary metric.
    *   Spatial Fréchet Inception Distance (sFID) and Inception Score (IS) were reported as secondary metrics. 
    *   *Note:* 50K samples were generated for each diffusion model, and the full training set of the corresponding dataset was used to compute the metrics. ADM TensorFlow evaluation suite was utilized for all metric calculations.
*   **Baselines Compared:** 
    *   *Data-Based Training:* Standard diffusion model training requiring full access to the original large-scale dataset.
    *   *Data-Free Training (0%):* Teacher model generates a large quantity of high-quality synthetic samples (matching the size of the original dataset) to form the training set. Student models are initialized randomly and trained using standard procedures.
    *   *Data-Limited Training (5%, 10%, 15%, 20%):* Integrates a fixed proportion of the original dataset samples with the synthetic dataset used in data-free training.
*   **Implementation Details:**
    *   *Teacher Models (Pixel Space):* Three pretrained DMs utilizing Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). Trained separately on CIFAR10 (32x32), CelebA (64x64), and ImageNet (32x32).
    *   *Teacher Models (Latent Space):* Two pretrained DMs utilizing CNNs. Trained on CelebA-HQ (256x256) and FFHQ (256x256). These were trained using a simpler loss function without incorporating KL divergence.
    *   *Student Models:* Maintained the same architecture as the teacher models but at a reduced scale.
    *   *Cross-Architecture Configuration:* Additional experiments were conducted crossing between CNN-based and ViT-based (Vision Transformer) DMs on CIFAR10.
    *   *Sampling Steps:* All samples were generated through 50 Improved DDPM (IDDPM) sampling steps in pixel space and 200 DDIM sampling steps in latent space without additional contextual states.
    *   *Synthetic Baseline Generation:* Synthetic datasets for baseline methods were generated using IDDPM-1000 for CIFAR10, IDDPM-100 for CelebA and ImageNet, and DDIM-100 for CelebA-HQ and FFHQ.
    *   *Objective:* The dynamic iterative distillation employed a specialized DKDM objective targeting both pixel and latent space training conditions.

## 3. Qualitative Observations

*   **Overall Performance:** The student models trained via dynamic iterative distillation consistently outperformed all baseline methods (Data-Free and Data-Limited setups) across the five evaluated datasets in both pixel and latent spaces.
*   **Surpassing Data-Based Limits:** In certain instances (e.g., the IS score on CIFAR10 and the FID score on CelebA-HQ), the dynamic iterative distillation method actually outperformed traditional data-based training. This suggested that neural networks struggle with learning the complex reverse diffusion processes inherent to raw data distributions, whereas the distilled generative distributions from well-trained teacher models presented an easier optimization landscape.
*   **Cross-Architecture Efficacy:** The dynamic iterative distillation technique proved effective irrespective of model architecture, successfully bridging CNN-based and ViT-based diffusion models. Furthermore, observations indicated that CNN architectures performed more effectively as compressed diffusion models compared to ViTs under these settings.
*   **Ablation on Iterative Strategies:** When tracking FID scores over 200,000 training iterations (without early stopping), the dynamic iterative distillation strategy demonstrated substantially faster convergence and achieved superior generative performance compared to its standard "iterative distillation" and "shuffled iterative distillation" variants. The convergence trajectory tightly matched that of the baselines, validating the theoretical alignment of the data-free objective with standard diffusion objectives.
*   **Impact of Scaling Factor ($\rho$):** Analyzing the batch enlargement scaling factor ($\rho$) revealed a saturation point in distillation efficiency. Increasing $\rho$ improved performance by affording greater flexibility in batch construction; however, beyond a certain threshold, the gains diminished, indicating an optimal upper bound for batch diversity requirements.
*   **Resource Efficiency:** The dynamic iterative distillation method required only minor additional GPU memory overhead while achieving faster training speeds within the latent space experiments compared to data-heavy alternatives. 
*   **Sample Quality:** Visual generation artifacts and high-quality qualitative outputs across all five datasets confirmed the student models’ capacity to closely replicate the teacher models' distribution without any real-data intervention.

prompt.text:
Role: Senior AI Researcher and Academic Writer.
Objective: Complete a machine learning research paper by filling in missing sections of a provided LaTeX template and generating a corresponding bibliography file. You must produce a scientifically sound, well-structured paper suitable for submission to a top-tier ML conference.

Inputs
You will receive the following materials:
• idea.md: Detailed description of the proposed method and technical ideas.
• experimental_log.md: Raw experimental results and observations used to construct tables, figures, and analysis.
• conference_guidelines.md: Formatting and stylistic requirements for the target conference.
• figures_list: A list of figures that may be referenced in the paper.

Conference Guidelines
# CVPR 2025 Paper Writing Guidelines

Below are the instructions to help you with the latex paper writing process for CVPR 2025.

## Language
All manuscripts must be in English.

## Submission Policies & Anonymity
CVPR reviewing is double-blind. Authors must not know the names of the reviewers, and reviewers must not know the names of the authors.

* **No Identifying Information:** Do not provide information that may identify the authors in the acknowledgments (e.g., co-workers and grant IDs) or in the supplementary material.
* **Links:** Do not provide links to websites that identify the authors.
* **GitHub:** Links to GitHub must be anonymous.
* **Self-Citation:** If you need to cite any of your own papers that are being submitted concurrently, include anonymized versions in the supplementary material and cite them as anonymous. Do not use the words "my" or "our" when citing previous work; treat your own prior work as if it were written by someone else (e.g., "Smith et al. showed..." rather than "We showed...").

## Paper length
Papers, excluding the references section, must be no longer than eight pages in length.
The references section will not be included in the page count, and there is no limit on the length of the references section.
For example, a paper of eight pages with two pages of references would have a total length of 10 pages.

Overlength papers, or papers where margins and formatting are deemed significantly altered, will simply not be reviewed.

## Mathematics
Please number all of your sections and displayed equations as in these examples:
```latex
\begin{equation}
  E = m\cdot c^2
  \label{eq:important}
\end{equation}
```
and
```latex
\begin{equation}
  v = a\cdot t.
  \label{eq:also-important}
\end{equation}
```

## Formatting your paper
All text must be in a two-column format.
The total allowable size of the text area is $6\frac78$ inches (17.46 cm) wide by $8\frac78$ inches (22.54 cm) high.
Columns are to be $3\frac14$ inches (8.25 cm) wide, with a $\frac{5}{16}$ inch (0.8 cm) space between them.
The main title (on the first page) should begin 1 inch (2.54 cm) from the top edge of the page.
The second and following pages should begin 1 inch (2.54 cm) from the top edge.
On all pages, the bottom margin should be $1\frac{1}{8}$ inches (2.86 cm) from the bottom edge of the page for $8.5 \times 11$-inch paper;
for A4 paper, approximately $1\frac{5}{8}$ inches (4.13 cm) from the bottom edge of the page.

### Type style and fonts
Wherever Times is specified, Times Roman may also be used. If neither is available on your word processor, please use the font closest in appearance to Times to which you have access.

### Main Title
Center the title $1\frac{3}{8}$ inches (3.49 cm) from the top edge of the first page. The title should be in Times 14-point, boldface type. Capitalize the first letter of nouns, pronouns, verbs, adjectives, and adverbs; do not capitalize articles, coordinate conjunctions, or prepositions (unless the title begins with such a word).

The ABSTRACT and MAIN TEXT are to be in a two-column format.

### Main Text
Type main text in 10-point Times, single-spaced.
Do NOT use double-spacing.
All paragraphs should be indented 1 pica (approx.~$\frac{1}{6}$ inch or 0.422 cm). Make sure your text is fully justified---that is, flush left and flush right. Please do not place any additional blank lines between paragraphs.

Figure and table captions should be 9-point Roman type as in \cref{fig:onecol,fig:short}. 
Short captions should be centred.

\noindent Callouts should be 9-point Helvetica, non-boldface type. Initially capitalize only the first word of section titles and first-, second-, and third-order headings.

#### First-order Headings
For example, {\large \bf 1. Introduction} should be Times 12-point boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, with one blank line before, and one blank line after.

#### Second-order Headings
For example, { \bf 1.1. Database elements} should be Times 11-point boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, with one blank line before, and one after.
If you require a third-order heading (we discourage it), use 10-point Times, boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, preceded by one blank line, followed by a period and your text on the same line.

### Footnotes
Please use \footnote{This is what a footnote looks like.
It often distracts the reader from the main flow of the argument.} sparingly.

Indeed, try to avoid footnotes altogether and include necessary peripheral observations in the text (within parentheses, if you prefer, as in this sentence). If you wish to use a footnote, place it at the bottom of the column on the page on which it is referenced.
Use Times 8-point type, single-spaced.

### Cross-references
For the benefit of author(s) and readers, please use the
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \cref{...}
\end{verbatim}}
```
command for cross-referencing to figures, tables, equations, or sections.

This will automatically insert the appropriate label alongside the cross-reference as in this example:
```latex
\begin{quotation}
  To see how our method outperforms previous work, please see \cref{fig:onecol} and \cref{tab:example}.
  It is also possible to refer to multiple targets as once, \eg~to \cref{fig:onecol,fig:short-a}.
  You may also return to \cref{sec:formatting} or look at \cref{eq:also-important}.
\end{quotation}
```
If you do not wish to abbreviate the label, for example at the beginning of the sentence, you can use the
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \Cref{...}
\end{verbatim}}
command. Here is an example:
\begin{quotation}
  \Cref{fig:onecol} is also quite important.
\end{quotation}
```

```latex
  \label{fig:short}

```

## Illustrations, graphs, and photographs
All graphics should be centered.
In \LaTeX, avoid using the \texttt{center} environment for this purpose, as this adds potentially unwanted whitespace.
Instead use
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \centering
\end{verbatim}}
```
at the beginning of your figure.

Please ensure that any point you wish to make is resolvable in a printed copy of the paper. Resize fonts in figures to match the font in the body text, and choose line widths that render effectively in print.

When placing figures in \LaTeX, it's almost always best to use \verb+\includegraphics+, and to specify the figure width as a multiple of the line width as in the example below

```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
   \usepackage{graphicx} ...
   \includegraphics[width=0.8\linewidth]
                   {myfile.pdf}
\end{verbatim}}
```

## Color
If you use color in your plots, please keep in mind that a significant subset of reviewers and readers may have a color vision deficiency; red-green blindness is the most frequent kind.
Hence avoid relying only on color as the discriminative feature in plots (such as red \vs green lines), but add a second discriminative feature to ease disambiguation.


## Important Rules 
* DO NOT change `\usepackage[capitalize]{cleveref}` into `\usepackage[capitalize]{cleverref}`, as there's no `cleverref.sty`.
* Keep the existing packages in the template unchanged.
* For consistent compilation across environments, all figures will reside in the `figures` directory. Always include the `figures/` prefix in your `\includegraphics` command. Failing to include this prefix (e.g., using `figure_1.png` instead of `figures/figure_1.png`) will result in figure loading errors during the build process.
* Always use the following author information placeholder in your writeup:
    * Ambitious AI Researcher, AI Research Institute, 123 AI Avenue, ML City, researcher@institute.ai


Critical Constraints
1. Scientific Integrity
• All reported experimental results MUST match the provided experimental logs.
• Never fabricate results, numbers, baselines, datasets, or metrics.
• If results are weak, negative, or inconclusive, report them honestly and discuss possible explanations.
2. Literature Cutoff Rule
You must behave as if the current date is: 2024-11. Do NOT cite or discuss papers published after this date.
3. Page Limit
The main paper is limited to 8 pages (including figures and tables but excluding references and appendices). Use space efficiently while remaining concise.
4. Template Compliance
• Do not modify the overall LaTeX style or document structure mandated by the conference template.
• References must be handled through a references.bib file.
• Use standard LaTeX citation commands (e.g., \cite{}). Make sure you ONLY cite keys that exist in your generated BibTeX code block.

Section Guidelines
• Title: Concise, descriptive, and memorable. Preferably under two lines.
• Abstract: A single, compelling paragraph summarizing the problem context, proposed approach, key results, and main takeaway.
• Introduction: Introduce the problem and motivate its importance. Provide necessary background context. Clearly summarize the paper's core contributions.
• Related Work: Discuss prior work addressing similar or related problems. Detail the relationship between existing literature and the current approach. Cite relevant baselines and influential papers published before 2024-11.
• Methodology: Clearly and pedantically describe the proposed method. Provide sufficient technical depth for full reproducibility. Use equations, figures, and structured explanations when appropriate.
• Experiments: Detail the empirical setup (datasets, baselines, evaluation metrics, and implementation details). Present results faithfully based on the experimental logs. Ensure any figures located in the figures/ directory are seamlessly integrated and referenced in text.
• Conclusion: Summarize the main findings and contributions. Briefly and realistically discuss limitations and potential future directions.
• Appendix (optional): Include supplementary details that do not fit within the main page limit.

LaTeX Quality Requirements
Ensure the generated LaTeX compiles flawlessly out-of-the-box. Avoid common issues such as:
• Unmatched braces or unclosed math environments.
• Duplicate labels.
• Unescaped special characters (e.g., & % $ # _ { } ~ ^ \).
All referenced figures must exist in the provided list.

Output Format
Your final response MUST contain EXACTLY two output blocks:

references.text:
## Problem Statement

The training of modern Diffusion Models (DMs) is heavily bottlenecked by an enormous requirement for high-quantity, high-quality data. Training state-of-the-art DMs demands billions of paired samples, which incurs massive data acquisition costs, storage expenses, and potential privacy violations. While Knowledge Distillation (KD) has been explored to compress DMs or reduce their denoising steps, existing KD paradigms are inherently constrained: they fundamentally require access to the original training datasets. Furthermore, standard KD approaches for DMs rigidly require the student model to inherit the architecture and weight initialization of the teacher model to prevent performance degradation, stifling architectural flexibility. 

A naive data-free alternative—using a pretrained DM to synthesize a massive dataset from scratch to train a new model—is computationally intractable due to the immense time and space required to fully generate realistic samples. Thus, the critical technical problem is formulating a methodology to train a new DM of an arbitrary architecture, from scratch, entirely without access to the original dataset or reliance on a comprehensively pre-generated synthetic dataset.

## Core Hypothesis

We hypothesize that we can transfer the generative capability of a pretrained diffusion model (the teacher) to a newly initialized, architecturally distinct model (the student) in a strictly data-free manner by distilling knowledge directly from the intermediate time-domain generative steps rather than fully synthesized realistic samples. By redefining the knowledge form as intermediate noisy samples, we can iteratively extract time-domain knowledge from the teacher's reverse diffusion process. We propose that a dynamic, iterative distillation algorithm will efficiently expose the student to diverse noise levels and samples, drastically reducing the time complexity of data-free training while closely mirroring the original diffusion optimization objective.

## Proposed Methodology (Detailed Technical Approach)

We will formulate a Data-Free Knowledge Distillation for Diffusion Models (DKDM) framework. This framework consists of a customized objective function to bypass empirical data dependencies, and an efficient data sampling strategy.

### 1. Mathematical Preliminaries and Goal
In a standard DM, the forward process adds Gaussian noise to a data sample $x_0$ over $T$ steps, producing a noisy sample $x_t$:
$$x_t = \sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_t}x_0 + \sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_t}\epsilon$$
where $\alpha_t := 1 - \beta_t$ represents the noise schedule, $\bar{\alpha}_t := \prod_{s=0}^t \alpha_s$, and $\epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)$. 

The reverse process relies on a neural network parameterized by $\theta$ to approximate the posterior via mean $\mu_\theta(x_t, t)$ and variance $\Sigma_\theta(x_t, t)$. The standard hybrid objective minimizes a combination of a simplified noise-prediction loss ($L_{simple}$) and a variational lower bound loss ($L_{vlb}$). However, both depend heavily on empirical samples $x_0 \sim \mathcal{D}$. Our methodology explicitly eliminates this dependency.

### 2. The DKDM Objective Formulation
We will introduce a teacher model with parameters $\theta_T$ (pretrained on an inaccessible dataset) and a student model with parameters $\theta_S$ (which can utilize an entirely different architecture). 

To eliminate the dependence on the empirical diffusion posterior and prior, we will force the student to replicate the teacher's learned distribution. We formulate the baseline DKDM objective, $L_{DKDM} = L'_{simple} + L'_{vlb}$, where:
$$L'_{simple} = \mathbb{E}_{\hat{x}_t, t} \left[ ||\epsilon_{\theta_T}(\hat{x}_t, t) - \epsilon_{\theta_S}(\hat{x}_t, t)||^2 \right]$$
$$L'_{vlb} = \mathbb{E}_{\hat{x}_t, t} \left[ D_{KL}(p_{\theta_T}(\hat{x}_{t-1}|\hat{x}_t) || p_{\theta_S}(\hat{x}_{t-1}|\hat{x}_t)) \right]$$

Here, $\hat{x}_t$ acts as a substitute for the standard $x_t$. We define $\hat{x}_t$ as a sample generated by the teacher model. Specifically, if a single reverse diffusion step is denoted as $\hat{x}_{t-1} = g_{\theta_T}(x_t, t)$, we denote a sequence of reverse steps from timestep $T$ to $t$ as $G_{\theta_T}(t)$. Starting from standard normal noise $\epsilon$, we obtain $\hat{x}_t = G_{\theta_T}(T-t)$. 

By utilizing $\hat{x}_t$, the necessity for ground truth data $x_0$ is entirely eliminated, allowing the student to continuously match the teacher's predicted noise $\epsilon_{\theta_T}$ and step transition $p_{\theta_T}$.

### 3. Dynamic Iterative Distillation
Naively assembling a batch of teacher-generated samples $\hat{x}_t$ requires $T-t$ full denoising steps, resulting in an untenable worst-case time complexity of $\mathcal{O}(Tb)$ per batch, where $b$ is the batch size. To solve this, we will engineer a "Dynamic Iterative Distillation" pipeline:

**Iterative Denoising:** Instead of generating full paths for each training step, the teacher will perform a single denoising step $g_{\theta_T}(\hat{x}_t, t)$, and the student will immediately learn from it. The resulting batch will be preserved and used for the next iteration step ($t-1$). 

**Shuffle Denoise:** Iterative denoising inherently causes the timestep $t$ across a batch to be identical, destabilizing training. We will implement "shuffle denoise": initializing a batch of pure noise, we will apply random quantities of teacher denoising steps so that the timesteps $t_i$ inside the batch perfectly map to a uniform distribution over $[1, T]$. 

**Dynamic Batch Enlargement:** To prevent the student from overfitting to highly correlated trajectories (non-IID batch samples), we will maintain a substantially enlarged active batch set $\hat{B}^+_j = \{\hat{x}_{t_i}^i\}$ at iteration $j$. The size of this superset will be $|\hat{B}^+_j| = \rho |\hat{B}^s_j|$, where $\rho$ is a scalar hyperparameter and $|\hat{B}^s_j|$ is the actual subset size used for a single optimization step.

During each training step:
1. We will randomly sample a subset $\hat{B}^s_j$ from the superset $\hat{B}^+_j$.
2. The teacher will denoise the samples in $\hat{B}^s_j$ by exactly one step.
3. The student will compute the gradient using these single-step pairs.
4. The one-step denoised samples will replace their older counterparts in the superset to form $\hat{B}^+_{j+1}$.

This reduces the complexity from $\mathcal{O}(Tb)$ to $\mathcal{O}(b)$ while vastly increasing the diversity of the distillation target data.

### 4. Final Loss Computation
Our final training optimization will execute gradient descent on $\nabla_{\theta_S} L^*_{DKDM}$, computed over our dynamically maintained superset:
$$L^*_{DKDM} = L^*_{simple} + L^*_{vlb}$$
$$L^*_{simple} = \mathbb{E}_{(\hat{x}_t, t) \sim \hat{B}^+} \left[ ||\epsilon_{\theta_T}(\hat{x}_t, t) - \epsilon_{\theta_S}(\hat{x}_t, t)||^2 \right]$$
$$L^*_{vlb} = \mathbb{E}_{(\hat{x}_t, t) \sim \hat{B}^+} \left[ D_{KL}(p_{\theta_T}(\hat{x}_{t-1}|\hat{x}_t) || p_{\theta_S}(\hat{x}_{t-1}|\hat{x}_t)) \right]$$

## Expected Contribution

This framework will fundamentally sever the dependency between training new diffusion architectures and possessing the raw data distributions they target. Theoretically, this methodology will demonstrate that generative reverse-process mapping is a sufficient proxy for empirical data distribution. Practically, it will allow researchers to construct, downscale, or wholly shift architectures (e.g., crossing from CNN-based backbones to Vision Transformer backbones) entirely in a data-free regime. Because the student learns from the smoothed probabilistic mapping of a well-trained teacher rather than sparse, noisy empirical data, we anticipate that this methodology will not only match standard data-dependent training but yield mathematically smoother convergence.

preinstalled.en: orchestrator image: upstream code at the pin (unmodified), uv-locked dependencies, the docker CLI (a shim adds proxy and CA to sibling containers); agent image: upstream's own agent-cli Dockerfile

notes.benchmark_paths: A benchmark item's paths are mounted into the agent containers unless upstream mounts the same path itself (/workspace and below, /home/agent-home, /task-source, /run, /tmp): those are left out and listed in logs/sibling-mounts.txt. The agents work in upstream's own /workspace (the run directory), so a deliverable the official prompt names under such a path is not written where the run collects it.
notes.venue: paper.paper_format=iclr for every task. The system has only iclr and alife specs and does not choose a venue itself; ICML and NeurIPS templates and a system-chosen venue are unsupported.
notes.task_input: Only the `# Goal` and `# Rubrics` sections of task.md are read: all five candidate files are put under `# Goal` with their headings turned into bold lines; `# Rubrics` carries a neutral line. The paradigm is optimisation of a scalar score: the task-drafting phase (documented as experimental) turns the brief into an evaluator and a seed program.
notes.phases: execution.phases=task_drafting,investigation,final_evaluation,paper; the system's own default also runs ablations and posthoc; final_evaluation stays because a drafted task requires it before the paper. review/revision (second model) are never selected.
notes.agent_pool: agent.pool and agent.models.* are left empty: one model for every phase.
notes.second_provider: No OPENAI/GEMINI key is supplied (concept figures stay in deterministic export mode).
notes.time: No global wall-clock or token cap exists upstream; the runner enforces time_limit_hours. Native caps used: idea cycles=3, per-phase timeouts from [systems.agentic-scientist].
notes.network: Sibling agent containers run on the shield's internal network; the agents keep their CLI WebFetch/Bash network, which go through the shield. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield.
notes.search: Provider server-side web search is switched off in every sibling by the agent CLIs' own system settings, bind-mounted read-only by the docker shim: Claude Code /etc/claude-code/managed-settings.json (permissions.deny WebSearch), Codex /etc/codex/config.toml (web_search="disabled") and /etc/codex/requirements.toml (allowed_web_search_modes=["disabled"]). Upstream's own Semantic Scholar client goes through the shield.
notes.key_exposure: The provider key is in the environment of the agent containers (upstream env-file mechanism) and therefore visible to commands the agent runs. Claude Code's CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB=1 was tried and aborts: it needs bubblewrap, which the unmodified upstream agent image lacks.
notes.gpu: gpus=1 is wired (container.gpu_count, harness GPU evaluation) but was not exercised.
notes.docker_socket: The orchestrator container has the host docker socket (root-equivalent on the host).

The paradigm is optimisation of a scalar score: the task-drafting phase (documented as experimental) turns the brief into an evaluator and a seed program.
notes.phases: execution.phases=task_drafting,investigation,final_evaluation,paper; the system's own default also runs ablations and posthoc; final_evaluation stays because a drafted task requires it before the paper. review/revision (second model) are never selected.
notes.agent_pool: agent.pool and agent.models.* are left empty: one model for every phase.
notes.second_provider: No OPENAI/GEMINI key is supplied (concept figures stay in deterministic export mode).
notes.time: No global wall-clock or token cap exists upstream; the runner enforces time_limit_hours. Native caps used: idea cycles=3, per-phase timeouts from [systems.agentic-scientist].
notes.network: Sibling agent containers run on the shield's internal network; the agents keep their CLI WebFetch/Bash network, which go through the shield. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield.
notes.search: Provider server-side web search is switched off in every sibling by the agent CLIs' own system settings, bind-mounted read-only by the docker shim: Claude Code /etc/claude-code/managed-settings.json (permissions.deny WebSearch), Codex /etc/codex/config.toml (web_search="disabled") and /etc/codex/requirements.toml (allowed_web_search_modes=["disabled"]). Upstream's own Semantic Scholar client goes through the shield.
notes.key_exposure: The provider key is in the environment of the agent containers (upstream env-file mechanism) and therefore visible to commands the agent runs. Claude Code's CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB=1 was tried and aborts: it needs bubblewrap, which the unmodified upstream agent image lacks.
notes.gpu: gpus=1 is wired (container.gpu_count, harness GPU evaluation) but was not exercised.
notes.docker_socket: The orchestrator container has the host docker socket (root-equivalent on the host).

preinstalled.en: python:3.11 bookworm; upstream code via PYTHONPATH; pdflatex + bibtex; CPU PyTorch with numpy, scipy, scikit-learn, pandas, matplotlib and more (pinned by constraints.txt)

notes.model: claude-opus-5-5 through the Anthropic Messages API (llm.provider=anthropic), no fallback models, reviewer model = same model. Requests carry model, messages and max_tokens only (no tools, no thinking parameter); ARC's per-stage temperature is not sent because the model rejects it, so the API default applies.
notes.agent: ARC is not a tool-using coding agent: its 23-stage pipeline, its own code agent and its reviewers are prompt chains over plain chat completions. conditions.agent=claude means only that the provider is Anthropic; Claude Code is not involved. Generated experiments run as a plain subprocess in the container.
notes.effort: ARC has no effort setting; usage-log.patch sends output_config.effort='high' with every request. Haiku 5.5 thinks by default and ARC's per-stage max_tokens (for example 4096) is shared with the thinking tokens, so long outputs can still be cut short.
notes.venue: Not chosen by the system: export.target_conference=iclr_2026 comes from [systems.autoresearchclaw].
notes.tokens: ARC records no usage. A logging-only patch (usage-log.patch) appends each Messages API `usage` block to anthropic-usage.jsonl; cost is not computed. The same patch carries the RWE_OMIT_TEMPERATURE and RWE_EFFORT switches.
notes.time: No global wall-clock or budget cap in ARC; only the runner's limit applies. Per experiment run 3600 s, refinement iterations 10, repair cycles 3.
notes.input: Chinese pack text goes verbatim (candidate files concatenated, with <!-- file --> markers) into prompts.extra_prompts of 18 stages. ARC takes one topic string and checks generated code against it, so research.topic is the candidate TASK.md verbatim with whitespace collapsed. Literature queries come from the stage-3 model plan; ARC's ASCII keyword splitter and its whitespace-based query expansion yield a few useless queries from the Chinese text. Starter papers are guidance text only: ARC cannot ingest seed papers.
notes.search: Web search, crawling, GitHub, HF Hub, Gemini and OpenCode are off. Literature search in stage 4 uses ['openalex', 'semantic_scholar'] through ARC's own clients behind the shield proxy; stages 8, 17, 22 and 23 (novelty, citation verification) always also query arXiv, CrossRef and DataCite; the shield date-bounds those API calls like the others (a late DOI answers 403).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: every request to api.anthropic.com is built in researchclaw/llm/anthropic_adapter.py:136-148 and carries only model, messages, max_tokens, optional temperature, output_config.effort and system, never a tools or web_search field; the OpenAI-compatible client (OpenRouter :online / plugins) is not used (llm.provider=anthropic), web_search.enabled=false, Gemini is only used by the disabled figure_agent.nano_banana. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so such a path would be invisible to the audit.
notes.secrets: Generated experiment code inherits the container environment, including the API keys (ARC offers no switch to scrub it).
notes.profile: project.profile=ml_generic is fixed for all tasks; research.domains is left empty because the literature screen rejects papers outside the stated domain (a theory task failed with domains=[machine-learning]).

agent.name: none
agent.how: no external coding agent: EvoScientist's in-process sub-agents (LangChain deepagents)

tools.permissions: think_tool, deepagents built-ins, EvoSkills skills and an execute shell; skill_manager not registered; no search tool

preinstalled.zh: 上游锁定依赖（uv sync --frozen）加兼容补丁 compat.patch；TeX Live（含 fonts-extra、latexmk）；给 agent 用的研究 Python 环境 /opt/research
preinstalled.en: upstream's locked dependencies (uv sync --frozen) plus compat.patch; TeX Live (with fonts-extra and latexmk); a research Python environment for the agent in /opt/research

notes.agent: No external coding agent: EvoScientist runs its own in-process planner/research/code/debug/writing sub-agents (LangChain deepagents) on the one configured model. conditions.agent only selects the provider; Claude Code and Codex are not used.
notes.model: Main agent, sub-agents and EvoScientist's auxiliary calls (tool selector, memory workers, summariser, graders) all use the configured model; auxiliary_model and model_fallbacks are empty.
notes.effort: Upstream hard-wires effort=max and max_tokens=128000 for Anthropic models. compat.patch makes the effort come from EVOSCIENTIST_REASONING_EFFORT (= conditions.effort); max_tokens stays 128000 (a cap, not a cost driver). Adaptive thinking (display=summarized) is upstream and not switchable.
notes.paper: The core writes a Markdown report (final_report.md); the EvoSkills paper-writing skill gives a generic LaTeX `article` skeleton with no ICML/ICLR/NeurIPS style and no compile step. The image has TeX Live (latexmk, fonts-extra) but no venue style files; the task asks for an official template, so a venue-formatted PDF depends on the agent obtaining the style through the shield. No extra pipeline stage was added; absent items are listed in result.missing.
notes.tools: skill_manager (git clone of any repository as a skill) is not registered (compat.patch); the Tavily key is not set so tavily_search does not exist; LANGGRAPH_CLI_NO_ANALYTICS=1; EvoSkills is baked in at its pinned commit. The execute shell and the EvoSkills paper-navigator scripts reach the world only through the shield; S2_DATE_CUTOFF is not set (the shield bounds dates).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: EvoScientist binds no provider-side search tool to any model (its only tools are think_tool, tavily_search when TAVILY_API_KEY is set, MCP tools from mcp.yaml, deepagents built-ins and skills; EvoScientist/EvoScientist.py:671-672 and 754-755 at the pin; the one bind_tools call is the tool selector's own output schema, middleware/tool_selector.py:166). TAVILY_API_KEY is not passed and the image has no mcp.yaml, so no search tool exists. Anthropic/OpenAI hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so a provider-side search would be invisible to the audit.
notes.credentials: The provider key is in the process environment and EvoScientist's execute shell inherits the environment (upstream has no switch); the key is therefore visible to the agent's shell. It is a run-scoped copy and is not logged by this adapter.
notes.memory: A fresh data dir per run (baked skills, empty memory). Memory workers, skill synthesis and the scheduler stay at upstream defaults, so their LLM calls count in the usage log.
notes.limits: async sub-agents off (README advice for scripted runs); recursion_limit=1000000; model retry wait in auto-mode 1800 s (time without progress counts as wall time); execute timeout 300 s per command. No token or cost budget exists.
